title: UConn’s Nik Khamenia to miss Duke reunion, loaded nonconference slate after foot surgery
content:
Fully whole, UConn (again) appears to be one of the best teams in college basketball.

That won’t be the case for quite some time, however, after the Huskies (3-0) announced Thursday night that sophomore forward Nik Khamenia will undergo surgery on his injured left foot. He will be re-evaluated in 6 to 8 weeks.

“Nik will have surgery in the coming days,” UConn coach Dan Hurley said in a statement, “and is expected to make a full recovery.”

Still, the 6-foot-8 Khamenia — who averages 10.7 points, three rebounds and 1.3 assists per game for No. 4 UConn — will now miss most of the Huskies’ upcoming nonconference slate, which is among the most challenging in the nation. Hurley’s team already beat No. 20 Michigan in a rematch of last season’s national championship game, but the Huskies will face five more top-15 foes — No. 2 Duke, No. 3 Illinois, No. 6 Virginia, No. 12 Arizona and No. 15 Kansas — before Christmas, as well as Ohio State on Friday.

That means Khamenia — a Duke transfer who played for the Blue Devils in last season’s Elite Eight loss to UConn — won’t suit up against his former team. The five-star recruit scored 7 points in 22 minutes in that regional final.

Khamenia injured his left foot in the first half of the Huskies’ 83-41 win over Wagner on Monday and did not return to the bench after leaving the game.

In Khamenia’s absence, freshman Colben Landrew will slide into the starting lineup. The 6-foot-6 Landrew, a top-30 recruit entering this season, has averaged 10 points, 4.7 rebounds, two assists and one steal per game as UConn’s sixth man. His presence ensures the Huskies’ starting five won’t see too dramatic a drop-off.

But that, in turn, will test the team’s frontcourt depth, which was already the biggest vulnerability for a group with aspirations of making its fourth Final Four in five seasons. With Landrew stepping in as a starter, Hurley will need much more from Russian freshman forward Egor Amosov, who has only played 18 minutes this season. UConn might also have to play smaller, relying on backup guards Junior County and Nils Machowski.

“If Nik’s not available for this nonconference slate, people like (Landrew) and Egor are going to now be thrust into bigger roles,” Hurley said Monday night. “That’s why I played Egor (the) majority in the second half, because if Nik is gonna miss Friday, potentially, or longer, he’s now in the fold. Depending on what Nik’s situation ends up being, potentially our margin for error would be thinner — but it’s not like we’ve got scrubs.”

If any coach can figure out how to weather a major injury, it’s Hurley, who has faced similar dilemmas in recent seasons. UConn missed Braylon Mullins with an ankle injury for several weeks last preseason, and the team was also without starting center Donovan Clingan for some time during its second of two consecutive championship seasons in 2023-24.
